summary.value:
Summary:

This paper presents a time-continuous, phase-less and biologically-plausible approximation of error backpropagation. It analyzes the impact of time lag in the forward- and error propagation and compares the timescales beneficial to model function to biological timescales.
While the topic is interesting and worth studying, this paper lacks novelty and does not acknowledge a whole body of work that tackles the same problems (see below). On top of that it lacks clarity in methods and result presentation.

strengths.value:
Strengths: 

The topic is interesting and I appreciate the goal of modeling a time-continuous system without the approximating step of discretizations. Additionally I like the finding that the time scales that prove favorable for model functionality seem to correspond to biological time scales.

weaknesses.value:
Lack of novelty and lacking acknowledgement of prior works:
- l. 42: "By contrast, existing algorithmic models are cast in discrete steps that alternate between inference and learning phases, effectively assuming that forward and backward signals are globally and instantaneously synchronized [1]". This is a strong misrepresentation of the content of the cited paper. This review paper compares 4 different biologically plausible algorithms for error backpropagation. Of which at least 2 (predictive coding as well as the dendritic microcircuit [2, 3]) do not rely on a split between forward propagation and error phase during learning. Also, while the review paper formulates these methods in time-stepped variant for ease of simulation, the original publication of [3] and some of the many publications on predictive coding models use time-continuous formulations of the models.
- Contribution 1: this is not novel as illustrated by the previous point. Other examples of pre-existing continuous time models are [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
- Contribution 2: the fact that learning in these types of models, which include either transmission delays or slowly evolving dynamics, is only possible if there is a synchronization and co-temporal arrival of error and forward signal, is already known. In fact, there exist already solutions to mitigate this limitation [4, 9].
- l. 135 "Unlike existing algorithms that explicitly separate inference and learning phases, these networks evolve in continuous time: outputs and weights change together in response to input and error signals". This is incorrect. There exist multiple prior works that emphasize the removal of a split between inference and learning phases (see above). 
- The related works section misses a whole body of work  [1-9]. These works attack similar problems as this paper and need to be discussed.

Lack of clarity:
- Eq 1: in the text the error is defined as "e" but there is no "e" in the equation. Presumably the notation there has switched to the "epsilon". This is unnecessarily confusing.
- Eq1: In the surrounding text the weights are parametrized as bold(v) and bold(w) (not capitalized) while in Eq 1: Capital (and not bold) W and V are used. This is unnecessarily confusing.
- l. 186: More details on the type of ODE solvers and simulation techniques used are required (e.g. in the appendix). E.g. pseudo-code would be good.
- The results are presented as color maps of accuracies, which is hard to read because of the big range of accuracy on the color-bar. Tables of top-accuracies would have been very helpful.
- Additionally, the color map plots are unable to convey a notion of variance between multiple runs, therefore neglecting the stability of performance over different initialization which is also an important information about a model.

Claims not backed by enough evidence:
- l. 137 - 161: The derivations/proofs of these statements should be detailed in the appendix. Without that these are completely unproven statement. Also, the paper assumes "Given the error eL as the gradient of the loss function with respect to the output layer". A huge part of the literature on biologically plausible error backpropagation is to investigate how this error signal is transported and shaped in a bio-plausible manner. Just assuming that the error automatically gets transported in the correct fashion leaves out one of the difficult open questions.
- The fact that the best achieved accuracies of the networks with multiple hidden layers in Fig 5 and 7 are inferior to the ones achieved by the single hidden layer versions, shows that this models lacks the capabilities to properly transport errors into the lower layers and make use of neurons in those layers. As a model/approximation of backpropagation this is however its main job.
- Comparisons to baseline models (i.e. MLPs trained with backprop) are hidden in the appendix even though, in my opinion this comparison is crucial to evaluate the quality of the model. Additionally, the results presented in these comparisons are very surprising. The approximation of error backpropagation, which has to deal with time-lag between forward and error signals and other non-idealities seems to consistently outperform the vanilla MLPs that are trained with full error backpropagation (even Adam instead of SGD). I find this extremely surprising and have the suspicion that a good hyperparameter optimization would change those results (in particular, just because Adam is used, that does not mean that the learning rate does not need to be adjusted).

References:

[1] Whittington, James CR, and Rafal Bogacz. "Theories of error back-propagation in the brain." _Trends in cognitive sciences_ 23.3 (2019): 235-250.

[2] Whittington, James CR, and Rafal Bogacz. "An approximation of the error backpropagation algorithm in a predictive coding network with local hebbian synaptic plasticity." _Neural computation_ 29.5 (2017): 1229-1262.

[3] Sacramento, João, et al. "Dendritic cortical microcircuits approximate the backpropagation algorithm." _Advances in neural information processing systems_ 31 (2018).

[4] Haider, Paul, et al. "Latent equilibrium: A unified learning theory for arbitrarily fast computation with arbitrarily slow neurons." _Advances in neural information processing systems_ 34 (2021): 17839-17851.

[5] Aceituno, Pau Vilimelis, et al. "Target learning rather than backpropagation explains learning in the mammalian neocortex." _bioRxiv_ (2024).

[6] Meulemans, Alexander, et al. "Credit assignment in neural networks through deep feedback control." _Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems_ 34 (2021): 4674-4687.

[7] Payeur, Alexandre, et al. "Burst-dependent synaptic plasticity can coordinate learning in hierarchical circuits." _Nature neuroscience_ 24.7 (2021): 1010-1019.

[8] Max, Kevin, et al. "Learning efficient backprojections across cortical hierarchies in real time." _Nature Machine Intelligence_ 6.6 (2024): 619-630.

[9] Ellenberger, Benjamin, et al. "Backpropagation through space, time, and the brain." _arXiv preprint arXiv:2403.16933_ (2024).

We thank the reviewers for their detailed feedback. We believe that many of the concerns of reviewers **SdJK**, **Fi2E**, and **vQom** arise from a misunderstanding of the intended scope of our work and our intended contributions. Our focus is narrow and specific: we investigate **whether feedback-alignment–style, weight-transport-free algorithms (FA, KP, DFA) remain functional when implemented as continuous-time ODEs with biologically realistic timescales.** To our knowledge, the viability of FA/KP/DFA under realistic propagation and plasticity dynamics has not been addressed in prior models, which operate under fundamentally different architectural assumptions.

Our paper does not intend to provide a general theory of continuous-time learning in the brain, nor to replace existing frameworks such as predictive coding, dendritic microcircuits, equilibrium propagation, or spiking surrogate-gradient methods. Our results do not compete with those models; rather we answer a distinctly different question about feedback alignment-style rules. 

Many of our reviewer’s (**SdJK**, **Fi2E**, **vQom**) critiques (absence of spikes, comparison to predictive coding and dendritic microcircuits, omission of eligibility-trace discussions) pertain to learning frameworks outside of our scope. We will clarify this distinction in the revised manuscript. We are grateful for the reviewers bringing up additional works, which we will cite in order to more clearly differentiate our contribution. **We have highlighted updates to our paper in blue text and additions in green text, to more clearly demonstrate the clarifications we have made in response to reviewers.**

In response to reviewer feedback, we also propose to **rename the paper** to more accurately reflect its focus, for example, “Does Feedback Alignment Work at Biological Timescales?” We are still open to suggestions about the title. 

With this clarified scope, our contributions are:
1. Experimentally tested continuous-time formulation of FA/DFA/KP algorithms
2. An analytic and experimental characterization of learning via temporal overlap
3. Evidence that these rules can operate robustly under biologically realistic propagation and plasticity timescales

We hope this clarification helps align our submission with the reviewers’ expectations. We will address their comments in detail with individual responses.

We are grateful for the time you spent reviewing our work and for your feedback. Our original manuscript may have been unclear about the scope of our contributions, which led to many of your misunderstandings. We have amended our manuscript to emphasize our actual contributions: the continuous-time biological plausibility of feedback alignment-type algorithms. As we discuss in the summary rebuttal, we also propose to change the paper’s title to reflect our scope more accurately. We will now respond to your comments point by point. 

**Weaknesses**  
**W1a:** 
> *For a manuscript on bio-plausible synaptic learning, the experimental setup is not appropriate: Only feedforward networks are studied and the input, output, and the task does not involve dynamics.*  

This is due to a misunderstanding on our paper’s scope: please refer to our summary rebuttal for clarity on our paper’s scope. We ask if a class of feedback alignment-type algorithms is feasible at biological timescales, so our experimental setup is precisely appropriate. As noted, we do **not** intend to study every possible biologically plausible learning model.

Recurrent architectures and intrinsically dynamical tasks introduce additional state variables and longer-range temporal dependencies. While these are important and interesting directions, they would expand the scope of the work substantially and are not required to demonstrate the core contribution of the paper: that biologically plausible error-propagation rules admit consistent continuous-time formulations with clear timing constraints and experimentally verifiable predictions. We clarify this scope and its motivation in the revised manuscript.

**W1b:** 
> *Rate-based neuronal units are important tools in computational neuroscience. However, their use here is not justified because millisecond-scale timing considerations are studied.*  

As mentioned in our summary rebuttal, our scope is to analyze whether heterosynaptic, feedforward, weight-transport-free rules (FA, KP, DFA) function when embedded in continuous-time dynamics with biologically realistic time constants. These rules are formulated in terms of continuous activations and modulatory error drives, not spikes or spike timing. A rate-based abstraction is therefore the natural mathematical setting for FA/DFA/KP, and has been the standard modeling choice in nearly all prior work on these algorithms (e.g., and explicitly mentioned in, Lillicrap et al., 2016; Akrout et al., 2019).

Please also see our response to W4a of reviewer SdJK. 

**W2:** 
> *If timescales are as given in Table 1, then separate activity and update phases appear justified. I believe essentially the same insights would be gleaned if separate phases were used.*  

This is a misunderstanding of both our goal and the mathematics. 

As described in our original paper and our summary rebuttal, the purpose of our model is *precisely* to study whether feedback alignment style learning remains functional when inference and plasticity evolve simultaneously in time, without assuming globally synchronized forward/backward phases. Discrete phases assume instantaneous convergence of signals before every weight update, a synchronization requirement that is biologically unrealistic and incompatible with physical limits (e.g. finite conductance speeds). 

The reviewer also confuses timescale separation ($\\tau\_\\text{prop} \\ll \\tau\_\\text{plas}$) with discreteness of algorithmic phases. Even with timescale separation, continuous-time dynamics produce phenomena that **cannot** be seen in a discrete forward/backward step algorithm. These are some of the core results that we demonstrate in our paper\! Timescale separation does *not* make phase separation an appropriate approximation for the questions we study. 

**W3:** 
> *All the findings of this manuscript on feedback delays are already known and formally studied as eligibility traces in the literature (e.g., Gerstner).*  

Please refer to our summary rebuttal. We thank the reviewer for bringing this confusion about our intended scope to our attention, and enabling us to clarify it in our updated manuscript.

**W4:** 
> *(line 146\) A key aspect of backpropagation is the back propogation of the error signal. Without showing the dynamics of the error signal, it would be wrong to say that the backpropagation rule is recovered.*  

We do not propose new dynamics for the propagation of the error signal, and we defer to previous results (heterosynaptic updates (Ziyin et al., 2025\) and discrete-time limits: DFA (Nøkland 2016 Theorem 1), FA (Lillicrap et al., 2016); KP (Akrout et al., 2019 section 5.2)) for theoretical proofs. Please see also our response to W11a of reviewer Fi2E.

**Questions:**  
**Q1:** 
> *In what sense their formulation advances beyond established continuous-time or eligibility-trace models in computational neuroscience?*  

As discussed in our summary rebuttal, our results do not compete with continuous-time and eligibility trace models. Rather we answer a distinctly different question that has not been answered in existing literature: can feedback-alignment style learning rules operate at biological time scales? And our answer does provide more biological motivations to investigate these algorithms biologically – an important contribution.

**Q2:** 
> *How does this framework relate to spiking backprop/surrogate-gradient methods (Lee et al., 2016; Shrestha & Orchard, 2018; Zenke & Ganguli, 2018; Bellec et al., 2020, Neftci et al., 2019)? Are there concrete advantages (theoretical or empirical) over these continuous-time, gradient-propagating spiking formulations?*  

Spiking backprop and surrogate-gradient methods answer different questions than our model; they are orthogonal, not competing approaches. Many works argue that feedback-style networks are plausible in the brain (Lillicrap et al., 2016). We investigate this possibility seriously with a continuous-time model that corresponds neatly to feedback alignment learning algorithms in deep learning, giving a way to study the effects of finite propagation speeds and other facets of continuous-time dynamics on learning through error propagation. See also our response to W3.

**Q3:** 
> *Since FA and DFA differ from SGD mainly in feedback structure, what is unified by casting them in continuous time?*  

See also our response to W2. Our work is not about unification. 

FA and DFA indeed differ primarily in network topology, and we do not intend to distinguish between these two any further. The motivation in our paper is to study the class of feedback propagation algorithms that includes FA, DFA, KP, and SGD in continuous time. As illustrated by our results, the structural differences between FA and DFA yield significantly different behaviors when implemented as continuous-time systems, due to propagation delays.

summary.value:
This paper studies neural model with biologically realistic timescale as a unifying principle. Despite the interesting motivation, the paper has substantial weaknesses, including: 

1. The conceptual novelty is limited: the main insights largely restate well-established results from eligibility traces, three-factor plasticity, and prior continuous-time learning frameworks, while the claimed unification of learning rules follows mainly from formal continuous-time limits of existing algorithms. 
2. The work is also poorly positioned relative to a large and directly relevant literature on spiking backprop and biologically plausible learning, with several claims overstating differences or mischaracterizing prior approaches. 
3. The biological and algorithmic grounding is weak: the model is rate-based despite emphasizing temporal precision, assumes idealized error signals without addressing error transport, and exhibits poor depth scaling. 
4. The empirical evaluation is limited to small, simple tasks and lacks sufficient robustness, noise analysis, and clarity to support the theoretical claims.

reviewer_concerns.value: While the authors make a clear effort in the rebuttal to clarify the intended scope, target, and claimed novelty of the work (arguing that several concerns stem from misunderstandings), this clarification does not substantially resolve the core issues raised by the reviewers. In particular, concerns regarding limited novelty, insufficient differentiation from prior work, and weak empirical support remain largely unaddressed. As a result, the paper still does not meet the bar for acceptance.

reviewer_scores.value: Three reviewers gave clear reject scores and expressed high confidence in their assessments. Their main concerns including limited novelty, weak positioning relative to prior work, and insufficient or unconvincing empirical evaluation, are fundamental rather than issues of misunderstanding or presentation. While the authors clarified their intended scope in the rebuttal, this clarification does not directly address these core objections, nor does it introduce new evidence or analyses that would alter the reviewers’ conclusions. As a result, it is unlikely that these reviewers would have raised their scores had they participated fully in the discussion.

We write to summarize our rebuttal and to clarify the main point of divergence between our goals and several reviewer expectations. **We believe that with the updates and clarifications we have made to the manuscript, we are convinced we have very satisfactorily addressed all the concerns of our reviewers.** We believe that those concerns were primarily due to misunderstanding our scope and intended contribution, which we have addressed in our revision.

Across all reviews, the majority of critical comments (particularly from SdJK, Fi2E, and vQom) stem from a misunderstanding of the scope and intended contribution of our work. Our paper focuses narrowly on the question: **“Do feedback-alignment–style, weight-transport-free learning rules (FA, KP, DFA) remain functional when implemented as continuous-time dynamical systems with biologically realistic propagation and plasticity timescales?”**

To our knowledge, this question has not been studied. Prior works on continuous-time or biological learning address fundamentally different algorithms with different architectural assumptions. Our goal is not to compare against or replace those frameworks. Rather we analyze whether this particular family of heterosynaptic error-feedback rules admits feasible continuous-time dynamics under realistic conditions. 

This distinction was not clear enough in our original submission. During the rebuttal we substantially revised our exposition to clarify the scope, and highlighted these changes in color in the updated rebuttal manuscript. Our original findings stand independently of spiking models, eligibility-trace theories, predictive coding, or dendritic-microcircuit frameworks. Many criticisms requested comparisons or integrations with those frameworks, but they lie outside our scope.

**Substantive reviewer concerns addressed**

* **Misconception about novelty:** We clarified that our novelty does not lie in general continuous-time learning, but specifically in analyzing FA/DFA/KP under continuous-time propagation constraints.  
* **Requests for comparisons to other biologically plausible algorithms:** These frameworks make different assumptions (instantaneous algebraic error propagation, symmetric connectivity, etc.) than the class of algorithms that we study. We have added citations and explained the orthogonality.  
* **Biological realism concerns:** We clarified the rationale for rate-based models, the biological relevance of the shallow architectures we study, and the mechanics of our evaluation procedure. We clarify that our aim is to explore plausibility of FA-style rules, not general neural learning.

**Manuscript changes in response to reviewer comments (highlighted in blue (edits) and green (additions))**

* Clarified scope and removed language that could be interpreted as overclaiming  
* Added citations and related work to better distinguish our scope and contributions  
* Clarified dataset and experimental methodology  
* Proposed a more precise title: **“Does Feedback Alignment Work at Biological Timescales?”**

We also highlight that reviewer Qo8u evaluated the manuscript’s soundness and presentation as excellent, and emphasized that the overlap analysis offers a clear, testable insight within a clean continuous-time framework. 

Overall, we believe that once the intended scope of our work is properly understood, the reviewer’s major conceptual concerns are resolved. None of the reviewers raised objections to the correctness of the results, and all technical questions were addressed fully. The misunderstandings primarily concerned the position of our work amongst broader literatures, which is now clarified extensively in the revision.

We are grateful for the time you spent reviewing our work and for your feedback. Our original manuscript may have been unclear about the scope of our contributions, which led to many of your misunderstandings. We have amended our manuscript to emphasize our actual contributions: the continuous-time biological plausibility of feedback alignment-type algorithms. As we discuss in the summary rebuttal, we also propose to change the paper’s title to reflect our scope more accurately.

We will now respond to your comments point by point. 

**Weaknesses:**  
**W1:** 
> *l. 42: "By contrast, existing algorithmic models are cast in discrete steps that alternate between inference and learning phases, effectively assuming that forward and backward signals are globally and instantaneously synchronized \[1\]". This is a strong misrepresentation of the content of the cited paper. This review paper compares 4 different biologically plausible algorithms for error backpropagation. Of which at least 2 (predictive coding as well as the dendritic microcircuit \[2, 3\]) do not rely on a split between forward propagation and error phase during learning. Also, while the review paper formulates these methods in time-stepped variant for ease of simulation, the original publication of \[3\] and some of the many publications on predictive coding models use time-continuous formulations of the models.*  

We thank the reviewer for raising this point and suggesting related works. Our citation to \[1\] in the introduction was a typo in our paper — we meant to cite the canonical works on error-propagation style learning algorithms, and highlight that they primarily rely on discrete steps and global synchronicity. This is now reflected in our updated text. Moreover, we refer to our summary rebuttal for an explanation on our paper’s true scope, and we emphasize that our intention is not to study every learning rule. 

We have added a short discussion on the relevance of \[2\] and \[3\] in our Related Work section. We would like to highlight that while the predictive coding \[2\] and dendritic error \[3\] models do not require an externally-imposed phase switch, they still model error propagation signals as infinitely fast algebraic terms, assuming that all synapses in all layers see the correct $\\delta$ term, and that no layer may update before deeper layers have sent back their influence. Our contribution is complementary: any physical neural substrate imposes finite speeds on information flow, hence motivating our study of finite propagation speeds of both inference and error signals. Moreover, we analyze how learning depends on the interaction between temporal overlap of input and error, potentiation timescales, and network depth, which are not addressed in the models surveyed by \[1\].

**W2:** 
> *Contribution 1: this is not novel as illustrated by the previous point. Other examples of pre-existing continuous time models are \[4, 5, 6, 7, 8\]*  

This is due to a misunderstanding of our scope. We thank the reviewer for bringing to our attention unclearness about our contribution scope. Please refer to our summary rebuttal. We have amended the wording of Contribution 1 and other text to make this more clear. Again, we do not claim to deal with all continuous-time neural models of biological learning.

**W3:** 
> *Contribution 2: the fact that learning in these types of models, which include either transmission delays or slowly evolving dynamics, is only possible if there is a synchronization and co-temporal arrival of error and forward signal, is already known. In fact, there exist already solutions to mitigate this limitation \[4, 9\].*  

Please see our summary rebuttal: we do not claim that this phenomena is novel, but we do claim that feedback alignment algorithms like FA/DFA/KP specifically have never been analyzed this way. Frameworks like Latent Equilibrium \[9\] do not address whether feedback alignment-type algorithms such as FA/KP/DFA remain functional at biological timescales, which is the central question of our work.

**W4:** 
> *l. 135 "Unlike existing algorithms that explicitly separate inference and learning phases, these networks evolve in continuous time: outputs and weights change together in response to input and error signals". This is incorrect. There exist multiple prior works that emphasize the removal of a split between inference and learning phases (see above).*  

This is also due to a misunderstanding of our scope. Please refer to our summary rebuttal and see our response to W1 regarding phase separation and implicit assumptions about propagation speeds and synchronicity.

**W13:** 
> *Comparisons to baseline models (i.e. MLPs trained with backprop) are hidden in the appendix even though, in my opinion this comparison is crucial to evaluate the quality of the model. Additionally, the results presented in these comparisons are very surprising. The approximation of error backpropagation, which has to deal with time-lag between forward and error signals and other non-idealities seems to consistently outperform the vanilla MLPs that are trained with full error backpropagation (even Adam instead of SGD). I find this extremely surprising and have the suspicion that a good hyperparameter optimization would change those results (in particular, just because Adam is used, that does not mean that the learning rate does not need to be adjusted).*  

As stated in our summary rebuttal, the scope of our work is **not** to demonstrate superiority of this model over standard backpropagation. However, it is very plausible that a continuous-time model slightly outperforms a discrete-time model with single-sample SGD. This is not due to a fundamentally better learning rule, but may be seen rather as a structural difference in how delayed error signals are modeled in the discrete-time setting. In the continuous-time network, every weight update integrates the presynaptic drive and the delayed error over the entire sample window. When a delay is present, the informative and misleading parts of the update are mixed smoothly in time, and the plasticity kernel effectively low-pass filters these contributions.

By contrast, in the discrete-time baseline, a delay ratio $r$ is approximated by assigning a fraction $r$ of the samples an incorrect label. This preserves the expected fraction of mismatched updates, but it produces substantially higher variance: each discrete-time update is either fully correct or fully incorrect, whereas each continuous-time update contains a proportionally weighted mixture. This difference alone can lead to slightly higher robustness in the continuous-time setting, especially on simple datasets, because the discrete-time model experiences occasional full-strength gradients from incorrect labels.

We agree that hyperparameters may affect the magnitude of this difference. We have swept the learning rate and have not found better MLP performance than that which we report. However, again, our intention is not to claim inherent superiority of the continuous-time method. Rather, the key point is that the continuous-time update rule and the discrete-time dithering approximation are not strictly equivalent.

**Questions**  
**Q1:** 
> *Can you provide more details on the simulation techniques that were applied? The text seems to imply that the step to a time-stepped system is never made and everything is simulated fully in continuous time. How is this achieved?*  

Our model is defined purely as a system of coupled first-order ODEs. ODE solvers integrate the equations using an adaptive solver with error-controlled steps. Importantly, this is different from simply a finer discretization of gradient descent. ODE solvers do not discretize the learning rule; they only discretizes the trajectory numerically, exactly as in neural ODEs or dynamical physical simulations. Adaptive Runge–Kutta integration (as we utilize) does not correspond to taking fixed algorithmic “update steps.” Instead, the solver chooses internal step sizes dynamically to satisfy user-specified local error tolerances, and these steps are not tied to any learning rule. Steps can vary by several orders of magnitude over a trajectory, for example, shrinking to microseconds during fast transients and expanding to tens of milliseconds in stationary periods. Thus, the numerical steps belong to the integration procedure, not to the model. We have added details on the solvers to our appendix. 

**Q2:** 
> *Can you comment on the variability between runs with different seeds and except for the weight initialization identical parameters? How stable is the system under hyperparameter changes?*  

Tables 2 and 3 report mean and std of training runs with multiple seeds. Continuous-time systems have a much larger set of hyperparameters than normal systems due to the many time constants involved. As our results show, the time constants play a significant role in the learning dynamics and performance of these systems. 

**Q3:** 
> *Can you explain why the approximation of the backpropagation algorithm in an unideal system (temporal mismatch between forward signals and errors) seems to outperform the vanilla error backpropagation algorithm in an ideal (instantaneous) MLP?*  

Please see our answer to W13.

We are grateful for the time you spent reviewing our work and for your detailed feedback. We will now respond to your comments point by point. 

**Weaknesses:**  
**W1:** 
> *The proposed model suffers from high computational complexity, which inevitably limits the scope of the experiments. While this fact is already acknowledged by the authors in their Limitation section, the empirical results can only offer partial support to the core theoretical claims. In particular one is left to wonder whether such technique could handle more challenging problems such as CIFAR-10/100 (or even TinyImageNet) where depth is necessary for accurate performance, which however in turn worsen then overlap condition, making the end result of the depth scaling uncertain.*  

Our goal in this work is not to propose a scalable training algorithm for deep high-dimensional datasets, but to understand the constraints under which continuous-time, feedback alignment-type learning rules can operate. These questions are orthogonal to the engineering goal of achieving competitive performance on CIFAR-10/100 or TinyImageNet.

The reviewer’s concern about depth is scientifically interesting but conceptually misplaced for our setting. In biological systems, most regions responsible for fast learning are indeed shallow: the cerebellum (which is the most iconic motivation for the feedback alignment algorithm) is often modeled as a 1-3 layer perceptron architecture (Albus, 1971). These architectures rely heavily on width rather than large feedforward depth. One insight that our results suggest is that continuous-time learning with finite propagation delays strongly constrains depth, because the update magnitude depends on temporal overlap between presynaptic drive and error signals. Our experiments illustrate this limitation directly.

Finally, although our networks are fairly low dimensional compared to modern deep learning benchmarks, solving these systems as stiff, multi-timescale ODEs with biologically realistic propagation delays is already extremely computationally intensive. Exploring ImageNet-scale architectures would require solving an entirely new set of engineering challenges with regard to compute, and would not be necessary to evaluate the claims we analyze in our work.

**W2:** 
> *The "no phase separation" claim seems somewhat at odds with the fact that evaluation requires freezing W, V and clamping e=0, which indeed operationally sounds like a separate phase. This fact becomes more relevant if one wants to employ such mechanism for a continuously learning agent with undefined training period.*  

This is a misunderstanding: “no phase separation” refers to training, not evaluation. In our evaluation we freeze weights and error pathways purely to ascertain that the model is correctly learning, in an apples-to-apples comparison with discrete time algorithms. Our evaluation procedure is a distinctly separate idea from the two phases of forward pass \+ backward pass traditionally required in error propagation learning algorithms. 

**W3:** 
> *No system noise stability is performed (e.g. small additive Gaussian noise to neural output). Given the complexity of coupled ODEs, resulting system robustness is hard to assess without proper experiments.*  

For continuous-time algorithms, one of the most important and interesting sources of error arises from time delays, which we already study in this paper, and that our results demonstrate that these systems are quite robust to. There are many sources of noises in biology, including thermal noise and ion-channel noise, which pose interesting open questions that we plan to study in the future.

> *The conceptual novelty is limited. The central claim that learning succeeds when input and error overlap in time is a restatement of long-established three-factor plasticity theory. The paper does not acknowledge this continuity or differentiate its contribution from that body of work.*

This concern is due to a misunderstanding of our scope. In contrast to those works, we focus on one specific line of biologically plausible learning algorithms, namely the error feedback network topologies and algorithms (FA, DFA, KP), and investigate their behavior in a fully continuous-time limit. The three-factor literature does not address these algorithms. Please also see our summary rebuttal.

This is a misunderstanding of our contribution. We did **not** claim that the unification/synthesis of SGD, FA, DFA, and KP is our contribution. We have rewritten this section to clarify this point. Please also refer to our summary rebuttal. Please also see our answers to reviewer Fi2E’s Q1: the ODE formulation is not the same as changing the discretization of stepwise rules.

> *Missing engagement with the spiking backprop literature. There is a substantial body of ML and comp-neuro work showing gradient-based learning in spiking networks via surrogate gradients or analytically derived rules (e.g., Lee et al., 2016; Shrestha & Orchard, 2018; Zenke & Ganguli, 2018; Neftci et al., 2019; Bellec et al., 2020). These already provide continuous-time, biologically motivated training signals and explicit analyses of temporal credit assignment in spiking dynamics. The paper neither compares to nor positions itself relative to these approaches.*  

Thank you for your criticism. Please see our summary rebuttal. Again, our intention is not to study learning rules that are not feedback alignment-type. We thank the reviewer for pointing out connections to other models of learning. 

**W4a:** 
> *The biological grounding is superficial. While time constants are drawn from plausible ranges, the model remains rate-based and omits critical biological features such as spiking and neuromodulation.*

First of all, many neurons do not spike (for example, those in the retina, many interneurons also do not spike), and the study of nonspiking neurons is biological and not superficial, and the time-scale is relevant: for example, neurons in the retina can have time constants at the order of 10ms, which is consistent with table 1\. 

Secondly, rate-based modeling is a standard mathematical limit of spiking networks in timescales relevant to learning, which is far slower than membrane and spike timescales. This is well established by biologically plausible credit assignment works, including Lillicrap et al. 2016 and Akrout et al. 2019\. We already acknowledged that we study rate-based models, which is a limitation we mention in our discussion section. 

Thirdly, our focus is on the feedback-alignment-type algorithms, and the original formulations of those models do not involve spikes. This is not a limitation of our work, but a limitation of the FA type algorithms. Extending these mathematical models to spiking versions is a challenging but interesting future problem.

**W4b:** 
> *The work does not generate new physiological predictions beyond known timescale requirements for eligibility traces.*  

This criticism is not quite true. Our main contribution establishes a high-level plausibility of this class of feedback alignment-style learning algorithms, and serves as a motivation to test these algorithms in biology. As mentioned in our summary rebuttal, our scope is distinct from the work on eligibility traces.

summary.value: The paper proposes a continuous-time dynamical systems formulation of learning in feedforward rate-based neural networks in which inference and plasticity co-evolve without explicit phase separation. Neuronal activities $z_l(t)$ and synaptic parameters $(W_l,V_l)$ obey coupled first-order ODEs with three timescales: fast propagation $\tau_{\mathrm{prop}}$, intermediate potentiation $\tau_{\mathrm{pot}}$, and slow decay $\tau_{\mathrm{dec}}$. Under timescale separation $(\tau_{\mathrm{prop}}\ll \tau_{\mathrm{pot}}\ll \tau_{\mathrm{dec}})$, several learning rules are recovered as limiting cases by suitable choices or dynamics of $V_l$ and local error definitions. The authors analyze how temporal mismatch between input and error modulates learning and derive an “overlap law,” showing that the essential feature for learning is that "input and error must be temporally correlated at each synapse". Simulations on small synthetic dataset explore delay tolerance, depth effects (propagation lags), and biological plausibility via chosen $\tau$-ranges.

strengths.value:
This work introduces a clean theoretical framework for continuous-time learning in biological rate-based network which recovers well-known learning strategies (e.g. Feedback Alignment) in appropriate limiting cases of the time constants and shapes of the error signals. On top of the welcomed unification of several previous learning proposals, the new framework offers a new intuitive insight for learning efficiency in terms of input/error time overlap. This represents a valuable/testable contribution.

The author also ground their modelling attempts on known biological constraints and - in light of their gained insight - articulate a new hypothesis for the role skip connections in deeper biological architectures: they are needed to preserve the overlap.

The work is in general well written with clean mathematical expositions and figure designs, with an easy-to-follow and compelling narrative.

weaknesses.value:
While we believe this paper represents a good contribution, we want to also highlight the following shortcomings.

1. The proposed model suffers from high computational complexity, which inevitably limits the scope of the experiments. While this fact is already acknowledged by the authors in their Limitation section, the empirical results can only offer partial support to the core theoretical claims. In particular one is left to wonder whether such technique could handle more challenging problems such as CIFAR-10/100 (or even TinyImageNet) where depth is necessary for accurate performance, which however in turn worsen then overlap condition, making the end result of the depth scaling uncertain.
2. The "no phase separation" claim seems somewhat at odds with the fact that evaluation requires freezing $W,V$ and clamping $e=0$, which indeed operationally sounds like a separate phase. This fact becomes more relevant if one wants to employ such mechanism for a continuously learning agent with undefined training period.
3. No system noise stability is performed (e.g. small additive Gaussian noise to neural output). Given the complexity of coupled ODEs, resulting system robustness is hard to assess without proper experiments.

questions.value:
1. In general, how would an "agent" address the problem of knowing when to switch on the plasticity? It seems that if one doesn't "manually turn off" the error signal in the model (i.e. effectively inserting a "no-train-phase"), then the synapses would drift based on whatever (random) error signals happens to impinge on the neuron, causing disruption to the network.
2. How would the overlap rule change if one starts to introduce "elegibility traces" that pick after the error onset or some other memory-like mechanism? Could such a principle be used to mitigate the problem with depth scaling?
3. How sensitive is the continuous time setup to system noise? Biological neurons are stochastic, so it is natural to wonder whether how resilient is this model to random (e.g. Gaussian) input or neural output perturbations.
4. The author propose that skip-connection might help overcome the overlap problem for deeper networks. Can you show a proof-of-principle scenario (by adding skip connections to depth-3 MLP layers) showing this effect?
5. Why does the continuous time model outperform the discrete analogs in Table 2?

summary.value: The paper studies learning in continuous time through a coupled system of ordinary differential equations for neural activations, forward weights, and feedback weights. Under specific timescale separations, the authors show that common learning rules such as SGD, feedback alignment (FA), direct feedback alignment (DFA), and Kolen–Pollack (KP) emerge as limiting cases. They analyze how temporal mismatches between input and error signals affect learning, proposing that successful adaptation requires temporal overlap between input and error at each synapse. Simulations on small datasets illustrate the influence of propagation delay, potentiation timescales, and network depth. The authors claim that this continuous-time formulation removes the need for separate inference and learning phases, yielding biologically and physically plausible conditions for learning.

strengths.value:
* The modeling framework is coherent and mathematically consistent. The coupled ODE formulation produces recognizable update rules, and the derivations are cleanly presented.
* The exposition connects well-known biologically inspired algorithms within a single dynamical formalism. This can serve as a pedagogical bridge between biologically motivated learning rules and continuous-time dynamical systems used in neural ODEs.
* The analytical treatment of delay and temporal overlap is technically correct and illustrated with simple examples. The results align with simulations and provide an intuitive picture of how propagation delays degrade performance.
* The empirical evaluation, though small in scope, is well executed and matches theoretical expectations. The relationship between potentiation timescale and sample duration is shown convincingly.

weaknesses.value:
- The conceptual novelty is limited. Continuous-time learning with eligibility traces and temporally overlapping pre- and postsynaptic activity has been extensively studied in computational neuroscience (e.g., Frémaux & Gerstner, 2016; Urbanczik & Senn, 2014; Izhikevich, 2007). The central claim that learning succeeds when input and error overlap in time is a restatement of long-established three-factor plasticity theory. The paper does not acknowledge this continuity or differentiate its contribution from that body of work.
- The purported unification of SGD, FA, DFA, and KP through continuous-time dynamics is primarily formal. All stepwise update rules admit continuous-time limits under small step sizes, so expressing them as ODEs does not constitute a substantive theoretical synthesis. The true differences among these algorithms lie in feedback structure and alignment, not in discretization.
- Missing engagement with the spiking backprop literature. There is a substantial body of ML and comp-neuro work showing gradient-based learning in spiking networks via surrogate gradients or analytically derived rules (e.g., Lee et al., 2016; Shrestha & Orchard, 2018; Zenke & Ganguli, 2018; Neftci et al., 2019; Bellec et al., 2020). These already provide continuous-time, biologically motivated training signals and explicit analyses of temporal credit assignment in spiking dynamics. The paper neither compares to nor positions itself relative to these approaches.
- The biological grounding is superficial. While time constants are drawn from plausible ranges, the model remains rate-based and omits critical biological features such as spiking and neuromodulation. The work does not generate new physiological predictions beyond known timescale requirements for eligibility traces.

questions.value:
- In what sense their formulation advances beyond established continuous-time or eligibility-trace models in computational neuroscience? 
- How does this framework relate to spiking backprop/surrogate-gradient methods (Lee et al., 2016; Shrestha & Orchard, 2018; Zenke & Ganguli, 2018; Bellec et al., 2020, Neftci et al., 2019)? Are there concrete advantages (theoretical or empirical) over these continuous-time, gradient-propagating spiking formulations?
- Since FA and DFA differ from SGD mainly in feedback structure, what is unified by casting them in continuous time?

summary.value:
This paper proposes coupled differential equations to study the activity and plasticity of neural networks. At the digital implementation level, this removes the separation between activity generation and weight update phases as all variables will evolve jointly according to the differential equations.

Using feedforward neural networks and rate-based neurons, the paper studies the impact of different schemes of delivering task error feedback to individual units, both theoretically for each synapse and numerically at the level of task performance. By analyzing the results of the simulations, the paper makes multiple observations on the neurobiology of synaptic learning, such as the delay between neuronal input and error feedback signals.

strengths.value:
- An ODE based formulation of neuronal activity and plasticity dynamics

- The paper consider three relevant timescales: (i) synaptic transmission, (ii) plasticity via intra-neuronal signaling cascades, (iii) synaptic weakening via protein turnover, etc

weaknesses.value:
- For a manuscript on bio-plausible synaptic learning, the experimental setup is not appropriate:
    - Only feedforward networks are studied and the input, output, and the task does not involve dynamics.
    - Rate-based neuronal units are important tools in computational neuroscience. However, their use here is not justified because millisecond-scale timing considerations are studied.

- If timescales are as given in Table 1, then separate activity and update phases appear justified. I believe essentially the same insights would be gleaned if separate phases were used.

- All the findings of this manuscript on feedback delays are already known and formally studied as eligibility traces in the literature (e.g., Gerstner).

- (line 146) A key aspect of backpropagation is the back propogation of the error signal. Without showing the dynamics of the error signal, it would be wrong to say that the backpropagation rule is recovered.

- In Eq. 2 and below, the role of the post-synaptic neuron is ignored. The concept of the eligibility trace formalizes this, which can be considered to either change the integration limits or shift the kernel function. In a 'continuous time' learning framework, what the integration limits correspond to in Eq. 2 is not clear. This shows up in a few places in the manuscript. For instance, the asymmetry considered around line 267 emerges from the "validation" of the pre-synaptic activity by the post-synaptic activity.

- For rate-based neurons and in a continuous time learning framework, it is not clear what it means for the neuron to be active in $[0,T]$ with $T \ll \tau_\text{pot}$.

- The paper studies two datasets: downsampled MNIST digits and a 'synthetic two-dimensional circles dataset'. The second dataset is not clear to me. More importantly, the tasks are not defined for either of the two datasets!

comment.value:
**Questions:**  
**Q1:** 
> *In general, how would an "agent" address the problem of knowing when to switch on the plasticity? It seems that if one doesn't "manually turn off" the error signal in the model (i.e. effectively inserting a "no-train-phase"), then the synapses would drift based on whatever (random) error signals happens to impinge on the neuron, causing disruption to the network.*  

Biological systems face the same issue: synaptic strengths drift continuously, and there is no clear distinction between a “learning phase” and an “inference phase” in the brain, yet perception and action remain stable. Neural activity converges on fast timescales while synaptic changes occur much more slowly. Our continuous-time formulation reflects this same separation of timescales: inference converges before appreciable drift occurs, so there is no need to explicitly “switch off” plasticity in order to avoid destabilization. See also our response to W2. 

**Q2:** 
> *How would the overlap rule change if one starts to introduce "elegibility traces" that pick after the error onset or some other memory-like mechanism? Could such a principle be used to mitigate the problem with depth scaling?*  

This question is orthogonal to the core direction of our work. We aim to investigate a model of continuous-time learning that most closely reflects the feedback-alignment style algorithms (FA, DFA, KP), which have no ability to account for interactions like eligibility traces. This is an interesting open question that we plan to study in the future.

**Q3:** 
> *How sensitive is the continuous time setup to system noise? Biological neurons are stochastic, so it is natural to wonder whether how resilient is this model to random (e.g. Gaussian) input or neural output perturbations.*  

See our answer to **W3**

**Q4:** 
> *The author propose that skip-connection might help overcome the overlap problem for deeper networks. Can you show a proof-of-principle scenario (by adding skip connections to depth-3 MLP layers) showing this effect?*  

This is an interesting question that is complementary to our core results, but not essential. Our contribution concerns the timescale constraints under which feedback alignment operates, independent of architectural enhancements like residual pathways. We are currently exploring experiments with skip connections, but we expect these results to be additive rather than foundational.

**Q5:** 
> *Why does the continuous time model outperform the discrete analogs in Table 2?*  

We do not claim that the continuous-time formulation is universally superior to discrete-time training. However, it is very plausible that a continuous-time model slightly outperforms a discrete-time model with single-sample SGD. The continuous-time dynamics of synaptic weights means that each update is similar to an exponentially weighted average of many smaller gradients within the presentation window. The dynamics act as a regularizer and yield something analogous to gradient smoothing, which may result in better performance than single-sample SGD in discrete time.

**W5:** 
> *The related works section misses a whole body of work \[1-9\]. These works attack similar problems as this paper and need to be discussed.*  

As highlighted in our summary rebuttal, not all of these works are relevant to our focus on feedback alignment-type algorithms. We thank the reviewer for highlighting these important works, and we have incorporated citations in our main text to better differentiate our contributions.

**(lack of clarity)**  
**W6:** 
> *Eq 1: in the text the error is defined as "e" but there is no "e" in the equation. Presumably the notation there has switched to the "epsilon". This is unnecessarily confusing.*  

We apologize for the confusion and have clarified the notation to use epsilon consistently.

**W7:** 
> *Eq1: In the surrounding text the weights are parametrized as bold(v) and bold(w) (not capitalized) while in Eq 1: Capital (and not bold) W and V are used. This is unnecessarily confusing.*  

In the figure we use the per-neuron variable notation with scalars, while in the text we explain that these variables can be stacked into the vector notation below. 

**W8:** 
> *l. 186: More details on the type of ODE solvers and simulation techniques used are required (e.g. in the appendix). E.g. pseudo-code would be good.*  

We have added more detail on the ODE solvers we used, but we leave detailed proofs and pseudocode of the solvers to the prior work that introduced them. See also our response to Q1.

**W9 & W10:** 
> *The results are presented as color maps of accuracies, which is hard to read because of the big range of accuracy on the color-bar. Tables of top-accuracies would have been very helpful. Additionally, the color map plots are unable to convey a notion of variance between multiple runs, therefore neglecting the stability of performance over different initialization which is also an important information about a model.*  

We refer the reader to Table 2 and 3 in the appendix, which report mean ± std. Colormaps in the main text are there for the purpose of highlighting the regimes of model performance, rather than to conveying exact accuracies on the tasks at hand. 

**Claims not backed by enough evidence:**  
**W11a:** 
> *l. 137 \- 161: The derivations/proofs of these statements should be detailed in the appendix. Without that these are completely unproven statement.*  

These are not our claims, but rather references to prior works. Under standard timescale separation, our ODEs reduce to the heterosynaptic updates (Ziyin et al., 2025\) and discrete-time limits: DFA (Nøkland 2016 Theorem 1), FA (Lillicrap et al., 2016); KP (Akrout et al., 2019 section 5.2). We have added text clarifying that these are not our contributions, and refer the reader to our citation.

**W11b:** 
> *Also, the paper assumes "Given the error eL as the gradient of the loss function with respect to the output layer". A huge part of the literature on biologically plausible error backpropagation is to investigate how this error signal is transported and shaped in a bio-plausible manner. Just assuming that the error automatically gets transported in the correct fashion leaves out one of the difficult open questions.*  

Our contributions are orthogonal to the question of how $e\_L$ is computed. We agree that the origin and shaping of the teaching/error signal at the readout layer is an important open question. In this work we make the same assumption as essentially all FA/DFA/KP and heterosynaptic two-signal models: we posit the existence of such a signal, and then ask whether a continuous-time, delay-limited circuit can use such a signal for credit assignment in continuous time. 

**W12:** 
> *The fact that the best achieved accuracies of the networks with multiple hidden layers in Fig 5 and 7 are inferior to the ones achieved by the single hidden layer versions, shows that this models lacks the capabilities to properly transport errors into the lower layers and make use of neurons in those layers. As a model/approximation of backpropagation this is however its main job.*  

Firstly, Figure 6 demonstrates that deeper networks with layerwise error propagation indeed achieve higher accuracies than shallower networks, indicating that the model does successfully propagate error signals to use deeper layers effectively. We do not claim that the continuous-time model propagates errors perfectly, nor that it does so better than discrete-time backpropagation. Our results do suggest that the continuous-time model is capable of successfully passing error signals backwards several layers in a way that results in learning.

Secondly, even shallow networks have high biological relevance. As discussed further in response to W1 of reviewer Qo8u, most regions responsible for fast learning in the brain are indeed shallow: the cerebellum is often modeled as a 3 layer perceptron architecture (Albus, 1971).

**W5:** 
> *In Eq. 2 and below, the role of the post-synaptic neuron is ignored. The concept of the eligibility trace formalizes this, which can be considered to either change the integration limits or shift the kernel function. In a 'continuous time' learning framework, what the integration limits correspond to in Eq. 2 is not clear. This shows up in a few places in the manuscript. For instance, the asymmetry considered around line 267 emerges from the "validation" of the pre-synaptic activity by the post-synaptic activity.*  

We appreciate the reviewer’s attention to biological causality and eligibility traces. Our goal, however, is not to model synaptic plasticity at the level of spike-timing-dependent, three-factor rules. As clarified in our summary rebuttal, the scope of this paper is limited to heterosynaptic two-signal rules such as FA, DFA, and KP. These algorithms are defined in terms of continuous presynaptic activity and a modulatory error term, and do not explicitly include a causal postsynaptic-gating eligibility mechanism. The integration limits in Equation 2 define the duration of a single sample being presented to the network.

**W6:** 
> *For rate-based neurons and in a continuous time learning framework, it is not clear what it means for the neuron to be active in $\[0, T\]$ with $T\\ll\\tau\_\\text{pot}$.*  

It means that during the time window of $\[0, T\]$ (for a given input sample), neuron $i$’s firing rate $z\_i(t)$ is approximately constant and nonzero. Because the potentiation time constant $\\tau\_\\text{pot}$ is much larger than the sample duration $T$, the plasticity kernel is effectively flat over $\[0, T\]$. Thus the plasticity mechanism treats the entire sample presentation as one uniformly weighted update, which is the flat-kernel approximation used in our overlap analysis.

**W7:** 
> *The paper studies two datasets: downsampled MNIST digits and a 'synthetic two-dimensional circles dataset'. The second dataset is not clear to me. More importantly, the tasks are not defined for either of the two datasets\!*  

The details on the datasets may be found in Appendix B. Both the MNIST and circles datasets are standard classification tasks. The high degree of linear separability of the MNIST dataset motivates us to also consider a more nonlinear dataset, that of classifying two concentric rings.

**Questions:**  
**Q1:** 
> *What are the tasks studied in this paper?*  

Please refer to our response to W7 and Appendix B for details on the tasks.

**Q2:** 
> *Would the results hold for a recurrent network model?*  

Please refer to our response to W1a.

**Q3:** 
> *Would the results hold for a spiking neuron model?*  

Please see our responses to reviewer SdJK’s W3 and Q2. 

**Q4:** 
> *Would the results change significantly if forward-activity and update phases were separated, as in common machine learning?*  

Please also see our responses to W2. Our experiments on delays and timescales would not be possible with the separation of phases. We expect that separating phases while still retaining continuous time dynamics should still work, but we have not checked this as it would be irrelevant to biology. This could be interesting as a future problem, and we thank the reviewer for suggesting it.
